## Exercise 1 

Create a vector of three elements (2,4,6) and name that vector `vec_a`. Create a second vector, `vec_b`, that contains $(8,10,12)$. Add these two vectors together and name the result `vec_c`.

```{r}
vec_a <- c(2,4,6)

vec_b <- c(8,10,12)

vec_c <- c(vec_a + vec_b)
```

Two vectors were made by concatinating values together then adding the two vectors together to get the sum. 


## Exercise 2

Create a vector, named `vec_d`, that contains only two elements (14,20). Add this vector to `vec_a`. What is the result and what do you think R did (look up the recycling rule using Google)? What is the warning message that R gives you?


```{r}
vec_d <- c(14,20)

vec_a + vec_d

```

The result was 3 vectors where r used vec_d's two vectors in sequential order and once it ran out of vectors to add to vec_a it 'recycled' or started over the order of vectors to then add. 

## Exercise 3 

Next add $5$ to the vector `vec_a`. What is the result and what did R do? Why doesn't in give you a warning message similar to what you saw in the previous problem?

```{r}
vec_a + 5
```

There is no warning here because were a just adding 5 to every value in the vector. A hidden structure was created to match the length of our object.

## Exercise 5 {-}

Generate the vector of even numbers $\left\{ 2,4,6,\dots,20\right\}$

**a)** Using the `seq()` function and
```{r}
seq(from=2, to=20, by=2)
```
The seq function allowed us to define what number we wanted to start and end with and at what intervals we wanted each number. 

**b)** Using the a:b shortcut and some subsequent algebra. *Hint: Generate a sequence of integers then multiple by 2*.

```{r}
(1:10)*2
```

I generated a seqeunce of integers I knew that when multiplied by 2 would have the same output of even numbers above. 


## Exercise 6


I set a parameter of where the values should fall and then how many elements there should be.

## Exercise 11 

Create and manipulate a data frame.

**a)** Create a `data.frame` named `my.trees` that has the following columns:

  + Girth = {8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0}
  + Height= {70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66}
  + Volume= {10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6}

```{r}
my.trees <- data.frame ( 
  Girth = c(8.3, 8.6, 8.8, 10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 11.0),
  Height= c(70, 65, 63, 72, 81, 83, 66),
  Volume = c(10.3, 10.3, 10.2, 16.4, 18.8, 19.7, 15.6))

my.trees
  
```
The data frame was created. 

**b)** Extract the third observation (i.e. the third row)

```{r}
my.trees [3,]
```
I used the data set to pull row three by using a formatting function where [a,b], where a pulls a row and b would pull a column. 


**c)** Extract the Girth column referring to it by name (don't use a numerical value based on column position).

```{r}
my.trees$Girth

```
The girth column was extracted using $.


**d)** Print out a data frame of all the observations *except* for the fourth observation. (i.e. Remove the fourth observation/row.)

```{r}
my.trees[-4,]
```
I substracted the fourth row by putting a minus sign in. 



**e)** Use the `which()` command to create a vector of row indices that have a `girth` greater than 10. Call that vector `index`.


```{r}
#which(my.trees[,Girth]>10)

index <- which(my.trees$Girth>10)



```

Using $ is much easier when trying to access the data like here when I pulled from the column of Girth to get row greater than 10. 



**f)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the large girth trees.

```{r}
large.trees <- my.trees[index,] 
  

large.trees
```
Similar to what I did in d, I used the notation above to only pull whatever rows that were associated with the index. 

**g)** Use the `index` vector to create a small data set with just the small girth trees.


```{r}
small.tress <- my.trees[-index,]

small.tress
```

Here, I just subtracted the index and I was left with any trees that had a girth less than 10. 

## Exercise 12 {-}

The following code creates a `data.frame` and then has two different methods for removing the rows with `NA` values in the column `Grade`. Explain the difference between the two.

```{r}
df <- data.frame(name= c('Alice','Bob','Charlie','Daniel'),
                 Grade = c(6,8,NA,9))

df[ -which(  is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
df[  which( !is.na(df$Grade) ), ]
```

The first method is saying to get rid of any value that is N/A where as the second option will keep anything that is not N/A.




## Exercise 14 {-}

Create and manipulate a list.

**a)** Create a list named my.test with elements

  + x = c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10)
  + y = c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51)
  + slope = 2.82
  + p.value = 0.000131
  

```{r}
x <- c(4,5,6,7,8,9,10)
y <- c(34,35,41,40,45,47,51)
slope <- 2.82
p.value <- 0.000131

my.test <- list(x=x ,y=y ,slope=slope ,p.value=p.value)

str(my.test)


```
A list was made but first creating all the objects you want in the list then putting them together using the list function. 
  
  
  
**b)** Extract the second element in the list.

```{r}
my.test[[2]]
#my.test$y
```
The second element of the list was extracted. 

**c)** Extract the element named `p.value` from the list.

```{r}
my.test$p.value
```

The element p.value was extracted from the list.
